# Decoding across transversal Clifford gates in the surface code

Decoding across transversal Clifford gates in the surface code Marc Serra-Peralta ,1, ∗ Mackenzie H. Shaw ,1, ∗ and Barbara M. Terhal 1 1QuTech, Delft University of Technology, Lorentzweg 1, 2628 CJ Delft, The Netherlands, and Delft Institute of Applied Mathematics, Delft University of Technology, Mekelweg 4, 2628 CD Delft, The Netherlands

Transversal logical gates offer the opportunity for fast and low-noise logic, particularly when interspersed by a single round of parity check measurements of the underlying code. Using such circuits for the surface code requires decoding across logical gates, complicating the decoding task. We show how one can decode across an arbitrary sequence of transversal gates for the unrotated surface code, using a fast “logical observable” minimum-weight-perfect-matching (mwpm) based decoder, and benchmark its performance in Clifford circuits under circuit-level noise. We propose windowed logical observable matching decoders to address the problem of fully efficient decoding: our basic windowed decoder is computationally efficient under the restriction of quiescent (slow) resets. Our ‘advanced’ two-step windowed decoder can be computationally inefficient but allows fast resets. For both windowed decoders we identify errors which scale sublinearly in d—depending on the structure of the circuit—which can lead to logical failure, and we propose methods to adapt the decoding to remove such failures. Our work highlights the complexity and interest in efficient decoding of fast logic for the surface code.

One of the many challenges in performing faulttolerant quantum computing is that of implementing a fault-tolerant gate set in a quantum error-correction (QEC) code. Transversal gates are an attractive way of implementing gates because they are both fast and inherently low noise. Although it is impossible to construct a universal transversal gate set in a single QEC code [1, 2], the Clifford group can be implemented transversally in both the 2D color and surface codes [3–6], leaving the T gate to be done by some fault-tolerant state preparation and injection. In the surface code some of these gates have been referred to as “fold”-transversal because they involve two-qubit gates between qubits in the same code block that are adjacent to each other when the surface code is “folded” along its diagonal, see Fig. 1. Because of this beyond-strictly-2D connectivity, transversal gates are particularly attractive in platforms with mobile qubits such as neutral atom qubits [7] or trappedion qubit chips (see e.g. Ref. [8]). The fault-tolerance of transversal gates has been known for a long time, but it has only recently been proven that transversal gates and magic state injections can be performed quickly (that is, with only a constant number of QEC rounds between each gate) without compromising the fault-tolerance of the algorithm [9, 10]. This stands in contrast with the purely-2D procedure of lattice surgery in the surface code, which can only perform a parity measurement on a subset of logical qubits once every Θ(d) QEC rounds where d is the distance of the code. Transversal Clifford gates therefore offer the opportunity for faster fault-tolerant logic—referred by some as “constant-time” logical gates [11]—but comes at the price of more complex decoding. In particular, in order for measurement errors to be correctly diagnosed, any surface code decoder must look at a syndrome record which has a temporal width that grows at least linearly with d [12, 13], 1. In other words, we need to decode across transversal logical gates. Because transversal logical gates can map stabilizer generators to products of generators, error detectors [15] may need to be set by the joint parity of more than two measurement outcomes. As a consequence, single measurement errors can flip more than two detectors, corresponding to so-called hyperedges in a decoding hypergraph [16]. Even in the surface code, the fast and simple minimum-weight perfect matching (mwpm) algorithm therefore cannot be directly applied to the full decoding problem. To overcome this issue, Ref. [10] used a minimumweight hypergraph decoder to prove their results. Such a decoder is inefficient both because minimum-weight decoding of a hypergraph is inefficient in general, and because the cost of the decoder scales with the depth of the

Inthispaperwemakeprogresstowardsdesigninganefficient mwpm-based decoder across fast transversal gates inthesurfacecode. AfterreviewingpreviousworkinSection IA, we describe our main set-up and concepts in Section II. We avoid minimum-weight hypergraph decoding with a logical observing matching (lom) decoder (Section III), which applies mwpm only to matchable subgraphs of the decoding hypergraph. Under a “basic” error model (defined in Section IIC), the lom decoder can correct any error of weight < d/2 in the unrotated surface code in arbitrary circuits with fast transversal Clifford gates and T gate injections which use fault-tolerantly prepared |T ⟩ magic states. This stands in contrast to existing hypergraph decomposition methods in the literature, including both “splitting” decoders and “hierarchical” matching decoders [17–21], whose failures we discuss in Sections IIIC and IVC respectively. One key detail in the lom decoder is how to handle so-called fragile logical measurement observables, that we discuss pedagogically in Section IIIB2. Our fault-tolerant results are not specific to mwpm and hold for any (distance-preserving) graph-based decoder, such as Union Find [22]. Numerical benchmarks of the lom decoder show high thresholds and accuracy compared to minimum-weight decoding under both phenomenological and circuit-level depolarizing noise and for both repeated and random logical two-qubit Clifford gate circuits (Section IV). However, the lom decoder is still inefficient because it has a decoding volume that scales with the depth of the circuit. To this end, we propose a windowed version of the lom decoder in Section V. It turns out to be non-trivial to design a windowed matching decoder for circuits with fast gates, resets and measurements, that is both computationally efficient and able to correct all 1 Note that this does not contradict the known existence of hierarchical cellular automaton decoders for the surface code which use local feedback corrections based on noisy parity check data, see Ref. [14] and references therein.

basic errors of weight < d/2. Instead, we introduce two variants of the windowed-lom decoder: a “basic” variant that is computationally efficient but cannot decode circuits with fast resets, and a “two-step” variant that can decode circuits with fast resets but is no longer guaranteed to be efficient. Both of these variants require further modifications to be able to correct all low-weight error patterns, one of which requires synchronized resets and measurements (except those in T injection circuits) to occur only every Ω(d) steps, but we conjecture that with these modifications both variants of the windowed-lom decoder can correct up to d/2 basic errors and have a noise threshold. We end the paper with a discussion in Section VI on possible future work, including the use of independent observer-decoders more generally in decoding. A. Previous and simultaneous work In Ref. [10], it was first proved and numerically demonstrated that one can implement fault-tolerant quantum logic by having O(1) QEC rounds after each transversal gate for, say, the unrotated surface code, supplemented by |T ⟩ magic states. The constructions in that paper and the earlier paper on correlated decoding, Ref. [9], invoked minimum-weight decoders or used decoders that can explicitly handle hyperedges, thus not necessarily being very efficient. Our goal here is to show how to construct an efficient fault-tolerant matching-based decoder. Ref. [23] proposed an algorithm to decompose hyperedges into edges (see also [24]), but we show that it does not perform well when decoding across transversal gates in Section IVC. Refs. [18, 25] decompose the hyperedges and iteratively run mwpm to achieve good logical performance. However, no formal guarantees are proven for the number of iterations and the logical performance for an arbitrary circuit and increasing code distance. Furthermore, the hierarchical mwpm decoding methods from Refs. [17, 19–21] cannot be used to fault-tolerantly decode an arbitrary sequence of transversal logical Clifford gates, as we argue in Section IIIC. Ref. [11] addresses similar questions of decoding as our work, with numerics decoding transversal logical gates such as the CNOT and H for the surface code, interspersed by single QEC rounds. Ref. [11] provides a windowed decoder, but it does not reduce decoding to a matching problem, instead it uses heuristic approximate solvers to deal with hyperedges. A limitation for this type of approximate solvers is their poor embedding into specific hardware for running real-time decoding. On the other hand, Refs. [26, 27] have already performed realtimedecodingonexperimentaldatawithgraph-baseddecoders, such as MWPM. We consider an arbitrary (unencoded) quantum circuit C compiled into |0⟩, |+⟩ and |T ⟩ state preparation, destructive Z- and X-basis measurements, and Clifford gates that may be conditioned on the outcome of those measurements. If a measurement is used to condition a Clifford gate, we call it a conditioning measurement; otherwise, we call it a final measurement. Each different set of outcomes of conditioning measurements leads to a different realization of the circuit. The outcome of the computation is then determined from some subset of the

We consider each layer of resets, gates and/or measurements to take place at a time labeled by a half-integer, so t + 1/2 with t ∈ Z. With this, we say that a circuit location is a point in the circuit in between layers of gates described by a set of coordinates (t, j), where t ∈ Z represents time and j is a qubit index. We make use of Pauli regions of the circuit, which is formally a list of Pauli operators P = [P(t,j)], with each element of the list labeled by a circuit location. Each element is itself a single-qubit Pauli operator I, X, Y or Z (ignoring phases). Two Pauli regions P1 and P2 can be multiplied to each other element-wise by multiplying the Pauli operators at each circuit location. We say that two Pauli regions anticommute if their components anticommute at an odd number of circuit locations; otherwise we say they commute. We also consider time-slices of Pauli regions denoted Pt, which is a Pauli operator acting on all of the qubits that are active at time t. Note that a Pauli region would be a Pauli operator if we associated a qubit with each circuit location as is done for space-time

We define an observable O = {M1, M2, . . . } as any non-empty subset of measurements in the circuit C where the outcome of the observable is the parity of the outcomes of each measurement Mi in the observable (the measurements Mi can be conditioning and/or final measurements and either X or Z-measurements). In a slight abuse of notation we will also use O to refer to the Pauli

Lastly, we define fragile, or unreliable, observables. The relevance of fragile observables relates to the encoded execution of the circuit C and the existence of fragile time-boundaries, see Section IIC1, but its definition depends only on C itself, as follows: Definition 1 (Fragile observable). We say that an observable O is fragile if its observing region O← anticommutes with at least one reset stabilizer S of the circuit; or, equivalently via Lemma 1, if the observable O anticommutes with at least one reset stabilizing region S → of

In the absence of conditional Clifford gates, a fragile observable always has a 50-50 measurement outcome, since applying the reset stabilizer does not change the state while it changes the measurement outcome of the observable. In the presence of conditional-Clifford gates, an observable can be fragile or not depending on which Clifford gates are applied, and can even have a deterministic outcome (an example is circuit 2 where the observable O4 is fragile if both conditional S gates are applied).

Fragile observables have been called “non-deterministic” observables in Ref. [10]. We will call non-fragile observables reliable observables. Note that non-fragile observables are not necessarily deterministic, due to the presence of |T ⟩-state injections. B. Fault-tolerant circuit implementation in the

Error model, detectors in the pre-gate frame,

For all results in Section III and Section V we assume a basic error model in the circuit C which is as follows: • independently apply Pauli X and Pauli Z, each with probability p, to each data qubit before each logical gate (followed by the single QEC round), • apply an X error (resp. Z error) with probability p before a physical qubit Z-measurement (resp. Xmeasurement). Thus in this error model, no errors are inserted prior to the QEC round, but each parity check measurement in the QEC round can be faulty due to the insertion of an error prior to the ancilla qubit measurement. We will show below that decoding efficiently across transversal gates is a non-trivial problem to solve even with this basic error model. Therefore, our strategy in this paper is to design a fast decoder that can efficiently decode errors in the basic model and prove its fault-tolerance (Thm. 1) However, these results directly bear on circuit-level noise since circuit-level errors have the same effect as products of a constant number of errors in the basic model, and we test this in the numerics in Section IV where we model more realistic phenomenological and circuit-level depolarizing noise models. One could also apply known heuristic decoding improvements to mwpm to optimize decoding for circuit-level noise, however this is not the focus of this paper.

outcomes whose parity is deterministic in the absence of errors [15]. In the absence of logical operations, each detector simply consists of two measurements of the same ancilla qubit in consecutive QEC rounds, as is standard for decoding memory experiments on the surface code. If the measured outcome of a detector differs from its ideal outcome, we call this a defect, and the full set of defects is the error syndrome. Given the definition of a detector, one can define its detecting region [15], namely the Pauli region obtained by backpropagating the Pauli representation of the detector as observable, defined in

In the presence of transversal logical gates, we wish to find a set of detectors such that the detecting regions are still local in space-time. Such locality is desirable because it implies that each detector can only be flipped by a constant number of errors in the circuit. Because parity checks are spread non-trivially by the logical gates, the detector definitions that achieve this, depend on the logical gates that are applied. In this paper we choose a so-called pre-gate frame for the detectors. In this frame, each Z- (resp. X-) detector only involves a single Z (resp. X) parity measurement outcome before the logical gate and a possibly non-trivial linear combination of binary measurement outcomes after the logical gate, see its precise definition in Section II in the SM [37]. A very similar frame choice is the post-gate frame where each detector only involves a single parity measurement outcome after the logical gate. These detector frames have been used in other previous works on decoding logical gates, see e.g. Refs. [9, 18]. Given an observable O = {M1, M2, . . . } of the bare circuit C, we can lift this to a logical observable O of the encoded circuit C by replacing each bare measurement Mi in O with a set of physical measurements that are in the support of the logical operator in C. Throughout the manuscript we choose a logical representative that consists of a string of X (resp. Z) operators along a spatial boundary of the surface code, as shown in Fig. 1(a).

on both data and ancilla qubits. The product of the outcomes of each of the physical measurements that make up O gives the raw outcome of O. The task of the decoder is to take the outcomes of all the detectors, predict the error that occurred, and then to infer which observables are flipped by this error. Combining the decoder’s prediction with the raw outcome of O gives the error-corrected outcome of O. Using the basic error model and the definition of detectors, we construct a decoding hypergraph G = (V, H) consisting of vertices v ∈ V for each detector in C. There is a hyperedge h ∈ H for each X or Z error in the basic error model, such that the endpoints of each hyperedge correspond to the detector(s) that are flipped due to the error 2. For each observable O of the circuit, there is a subset of the hyperedges HO that cause a flip to the observable, we call this subset of hyperedges collectively the observing hyperedge set, namely HO is the set of hyperedges that correspond to an error that anticommutes with the logical observing region O

Let’s discuss the structure of the decoding hypergraph G for our basic error model. It consists of both space-like hyperedges—those arising from data-qubit errors—that connect detectors at the same time-step, and time-like hyperedges—those arising from measurement errors— that connect detectors in two adjacent time-steps, see Fig. 2. At each circuit location (t, j), the space-like hyperedges form an identical subgraph consisting of a disconnected X- and Z-component corresponding to the Xand Z-detectors. Somespace-likehyperedgeshaveweight one, i.e. they are connected to only one vertex, and these we say are connected to the boundary. 1. Time-like hyperedges and fragile time-boundaries The time-like hyperedges may touch one, two or three vertices, as shown in Fig. 2. In particular, weight-one time-like edges correspond to measurement errors in Z- (resp. X-) detectors immediately following a |+⟩⊗n (resp. |0⟩⊗n) reset, or immediately preceding an X- (resp. Z-) measurement, and they will also later appear when we consider windowed decoding in Section V. In general, we refer to these weight-one edges collectively as constituting an open time-boundary (as a single defect can be matched to it), as opposed to a closed time-boundary to which a single defect cannot be matched. More specifically, if the open time-boundary arises from a reset or measurement (instead of from windowed decoding), we refer to it as a fragile time-boundary. Open time boundaries are potentially dangerous for decoding since only one type of stabilizer has a fixed eigenvalue. Moreover, the observing edge set of any fragile observable, see Definition 1, “borders” at least one fragile time boundary, in the sense that at least one hyperedge in the observing edge set shares a vertex with at least one edge in the fragile time boundary. How to avoid decoding fragile observables will be discussed in Section IIIB2. A weight-three time-like edge corresponds to a measurement error on an ancillary qubit immediately following a logical S or CNOT gate. For example, a measurement error on an ancilla qubit measuring a Z-check immediately following an S gate triggers three detectors: two Z-detectors before and after the measurement and an X-detector before the measurement whose detecting region includes the ancilla measurement by the definition of the pre-gate frame, see Tab. I from SM [37] and the gray hyperedge in Fig. 3(b). Clearly, in the absence of the weight-3 time-like hyperedges, G would be matchable and thus decodable using mwpm. Consequently, with just the weight-2 error pattern shown in Fig. 3(c), the matching decoder on Gmatchable will make a logical error. We demonstrate this numerically in Section IVC. We therefore require a different approach to decode G using mwpm, which we present in the following section. III. LOGICAL OBSERVABLE MATCHING

In this section we design a matching-based decoder for the hypergraph G. The key observation enabling our decoder is that for any single observable O, it is possible to define a matchable subgraph that “follows” the observing region O← of the observable. Therefore, by performing matching on this subgraph of the decoding graph, we are able to determine if a logical error occurred that flips the observable O. We call this decoder the Single Logical Observable Matching decoder, or single-lom for short. In Section IIIB, we turn the single-lom decoder into the lom decoder: a windowless matching decoder for the full circuit C that works by running a separate iteration of the single-lom decoder for each of the independent reliable observables in the circuit. A. Single logical observable matching decoding Given an observable O, we define the subgraph GO = (VO , EO ) of G as follows, see the example circuit in Fig. 4. To define the vertex subset VO ⊆ V, we take the observing edge set HO of O, which consists of a set of space-like edges on the spatial boundary of the surface code. Each edge e ∈ HO is connected to the boundary, with its only endpoint a vertex that occurs at some logical circuit location (t, j) and corresponds to an Xor a Z-detector. To construct the vertex subset VO , we include all vertices that occur at the same logical circuit location (t, j) and correspond to a detector of the same Pauli type as an edge in HO , as shown in Fig. 4. Given the vertex subset VO we now define the edge subset EO = {h ∩ VO : h ∈ H, h ∩ VO ̸= ∅}, which is intuitively the “projection” of the hyperedges in H onto the vertex subset VO , and H0 ⊆ E0. It is a straightforward exercise to verify that EO is indeed a set of edges for all possible choices of observables for the {H, S, CNOT} gates, by visual inspection using Fig. 4. A general mathematical argument can be found in Section III in the SM [37]. The single-lom decoder then proceeds by applying mwpm to the observed defects in VO using the edges in EO . If the returned minimum-weight solution contains an odd number of edges in the observing edge set HO , then the single-lom decoder predicts that the observable has been flipped by the error and must be corrected; otherwise, it predicts that the observable has not

Theorem 1 (Fault-tolerance of single-lom). Given a reliable observable O, the single-lom decoder applied to the decoding subgraph GO = (VO , EO ) can correctly predict whether any basic error of weight w < d/2 has flipped

The errors that occur on the hypergraph can be projected onto the decoding subgraph, let us write ⃗e ⊆ EO as the set of edges in GO that have been flipped. The defects that are visible to the decoder are then ∂⃗e ⊆ VO . The single-lom decoder then works by applying the minimum weight correction ⃗c ⊆ EO to the defects such that ∂⃗c = ∂⃗e. The total error-plus-correction string ⃗e ⊕⃗c does not trigger any detectors, and therefore is either a logical error or logically trivial, depending on whether ⃗e ⊕ ⃗c intersects the observing edge set HO an odd or an even number of times (respectively). We will now show that if the weight w(⃗e) of ⃗e is less than d/2, then ⃗e ⊕ ⃗c intersects HO an even number of times. First, note that because ⃗c is a minimum-weight correction to ∂⃗e, then we have w(⃗e⊕⃗c) ≤ w(⃗e)+w(⃗c) < d. Because the observable is reliable, all the time boundaries in GO are closed and the only weight-one edges in GO are the spatial boundaries on the surface code, with the observing edge set HO containing all the weight-one edges on one of these boundaries. If ⃗e ⊕ ⃗c were to intersect HO an odd number of times, it therefore must traverse from the “top” to the “bottom” spatial boundary. However, the minimum-weight path from the “top” spatial boundary to the “bottom” has weight d; this is even the case in the presence of time-like edges arising from weight-3 hyperedges because these edges connect vertices with the same spatial coordinates. Therefore, any possible string ⃗e ⊕ ⃗c that intersects HO an odd number of times must use at least d edges. This is a contradiction since w(⃗e ⊕ ⃗c) ≥ d, and hence ⃗e ⊕ ⃗c is logically trivial, and the proof is complete. Interestingly, there exist error patterns of weight at least d that are undetectable errors in the single-lom, but are detectable in the full decoding hypergraph and therefore may be correctable by a minimum weight hypergraph decoder. For example, if the error string uses an edge that corresponds to a hyperedge in the full decoding hypergraph, the string may be detectable in the full hypergraph but not in the single-lom. B. Multiple logical observable matching decoding In this section, we explain how to turn the single-lom decoder into a decoder for an entire quantum circuit C which we call the lom decoder. We start by discussing how to decode reliable circuits—that is, circuits in which all observables are reliable—before arguing that fragile observables do not need to be decoded in Section IIIB2.

In the case where all observables in the circuit are reliable, the lom decoder is simple: decode every logical measurement individually—both conditioning as well as final measurements—using an independent instance of the single-lom decoder. Since we only decode reliable observables, each instance of the single-lom decoder can correct every basic error of weight < d/2. Therefore, the lom decoder also has this property for the full reliable

It is worth discussing some properties of the lom decoder. First, the lom decoder does not pass any information between each instance of the single-lom decoder. Thus, measurements that occur at the same time can be decoded in parallel. A disadvantage however is that the same location in the circuit is typically decoded multiple times by independent instances of the single-lom decoder, increasing the total space-time cost of the decoder in classical hardware. Another important property of the lom decoder is that it does not explicitly provide a physical correction, i.e. a set of errors consistent with the syndrome, as corrections returned by each single-lom decoder may not be consistent with each other. This independence also poses issues for decoding near fragile time-boundaries as we will see when handling fragile observables in Section IIIB2, and when developing a windowed decoder in Section V. One can easily generalize the preceding definition of the lom decoder, and run single-lom decoder instances over any independent generating set of reliable observables—that is, any minimal set of reliable observables that generates all possible reliable observables in the circuit. The independence here is desirable since the single-lom decoder may not return consistent results for observables that are dependent on each other if there are more than d/2 errors in the lom decoding volume. For example, in Fig. 5, the single-lom decoder predicts a flip to O1 but not to O2 or O3, despite the fact that O3 = O1O2. Hence, if in the final measurements of some algorithm, the final outcome is some xor of final measurements, it is advisable to include this as an observable in the generating set to minimize its logical error rate, see the numerical evidence for this choice of decoding in Section IVD2. This freedom to decode a circuit using any set of (independent) reliable observables is also relevant for handling fragile observables as discussed in the next

Before going into this, we note that more realistic circuit-level noise will introduce new hyperedges in the decoding subgraph GO for the observable O and can make HO an observing hyperedge set. However, such hyperedges are decomposable via splitting into a constant number of edges that are already present in the decoding subgraph GO , see Section IVB, or decoding GO can be done with other hypergraph decoding techniques, see

Let’s first understand what the problem is when we decode fragile observables using the single-lom decoder, before we argue that for any circuit we only need to decode an independent generating set of reliable observables. The issue arises due to a combination of two factors. The first of these is a transversal logical reset providing a fragile (open) time-boundary (defined in Section IIC1) that is followed by a non-trivial logical gate after only O(1) QEC rounds. Second, we decode the corresponding fragile time-boundary multiple times by independent instances of the single lom decoder. If either of these factors are removed, no issues arise for fragile observables. The issue is closely related to those explored in other recent works [10, 11]. Recall that a fragile observable O is such that O← anticommutes with a reset stabilizer S, see Definition 1 and Lemma 1. Because O← anticommutes with S, this also means that the corresponding logical observing region

Because the observable is fragile, the observing edge set has odd overlap with the edges contained in the X-space-time stabilizer. as shown in Fig. 6(a, b)4. This leads to a somewhat paradoxical statement: applying the weight-2 space-time stabilizercausesanundetectableflipinthedecodedoutcome of the fragile logical observable O. Since it is a space-time stabilizer, applying it does not change the state at that time-step in the circuit, and therefore it cannot change the measurement statistics of any observable. As a result this operator does not constitute a logical fault. It does, however, still flip the decoded outcome of O—this is possible since the statistics of O are 50-50. To illustrate this point, suppose that a weight-one error occurred on one of the two edges contained in the space-time stabilizer, as shown in Fig. 6(c). Then, a decoder has two equally-likely corrections it can make, one of which flips the observable and the other of which does not. At this point, such an ambiguity is not a problem, since the decision the decoder makes does not change the measurement statistics of the observable. A problem does arise, however, when the same fragile time boundary is decoded multiple times by independent instances of a decoder, and the decoder makes a different correction in each of these iterations, while the outcomes of the logical observables are supposed to be correlated. Care must therefore be taken to ensure that the decoder decodes all fragile observables in a consistent way. To illustrate the problem, consider a pair of fragile observables O1 and O2 whose observing regions both border the same fragile time boundary but whose product is not fragile. A simple example is given by the circuit

in which the observables O1 = {M1} and O2 = {M2} are both fragile, but their product O3 = {M1, M2} is not. Moreover, in this circuit, O3 has a deterministic +1 measurement outcome. Now, suppose that we use two instances of single-lom decoders to decode O1 and O2, and take their product to infer the outcome of O3. Because O1 and O2 arefragile, alow-weighterror (< d/2) can cause them to flip. For example, the decoder may correctly infer O1 but incorrectly infer O2. This then leads to a flip—and this time a genuine logical error— to the product operator O3 = O1O2, even though O3 is not fragile. (2) causes an issue both for the lom and a minimum-weight decoder, because the decoder needs to be run, first to decide on an outcome for the fragile observable O1, and then a second time to decide on an outcome for the fragile observable O2. This is inherently a problem because a logical error to O3 means that an error has occurred somewhere in the observing region O← 3 , and every possible location has a non-trivial effect on the state of the system. Indeed, in Eq. (2), an error to O3 is consistent with an X-error after the first T-injection, meaning that the final state is S†T XT |+⟩ = S† |+⟩, which has 50-50 measurement statistics when measured in the X-basis. There are multiple solutions to this problem. Perhaps the simplest is to wait Θ(d) rounds after the transversal logical reset, allowing the state to reach the “quiescent” state [39], and perform an initial window of decoding that commits to a correction in the first Θ(d) rounds. This works because all of the subsequent instances of the decoder will use the same correction in the vicinity of the fragile time-boundary. In the case of the minimumweight decoder, Ref. Related issues around T-injections in the context of a windowed decoder can also be solved by using an additional ancilla per T-injection as proposed in Ref. [11]. Here, we provide yet another solution that is tailored to the lom decoder. To decode the circuit in Eq. (2) using the lom decoder, we use essentially the same procedure as for Eq. (1). We begin by applying the circuit up to and including the measurement M1. Conventional wisdom would now say that we need to decode the observable O1 and commit to applying the conditional S gate or not. However, because O1 is fragile, it can be flipped by a space-time stabilizer without causing a logical error. There is therefore no need to apply a decoder to O1, and we can uniformly at random select an outcome for O1 without decoding it, regardless of what the “true” outcome of the measurement was. Then, we continue executing the circuit up to and including the second measurement M2. The observable O2 = {M2} is also fragile and has a 50-50 measurement outcome. However, the product O3 = O1O2 is not fragile and must be decoded. We therefore decode the observable O3 = {M1, M2}, which is “peeled” off the fragile time-boundary, and infer the value of O2 from the product O2 = O1O3. We can then finish running the circuit, but we now have to interpret the final observable O4. As mentioned, O4 may or may not be fragile depending on how many of the conditional S-gates have been applied. If it is not fragile, it can be decoded directly;

if it is fragile, we first decode the product observable O1O4 = {M1, M3}, and then multiply its outcome with the outcome of O1 to obtain the outcome of O4. In all cases, only a basic error of weight > d/2 can cause a flip in the outcome of O4. We can generalise the procedure as follows. Each time a measurement M occurs in the circuit, we first check whether the observable O = {M } is fragile or not. If O is reliable, then we simply decode it using the singlelom decoder and continue. If on the other hand O is fragile, we check whether there exists a product with another, earlier fragile observable O′ (which can itself be a product of individually measured observables) such that OO′ is reliable. If no such O′ exists, we uniformly at random select an outcome for O and continue. If such an O′ does exist, then we decode OO′ and use the outcome of O′ to infer the outcome of O. Continuing this way through the circuit allows us to reproduce the measurement statistics of the original circuit fault-tolerantly, without ever decoding a fragile observable. Note that there is no guarantee on the minimum weight of such an operator O′, which we will find later to cause problems with the efficiency of the windowed-lom decoder in

In many cases, we do not need to actually randomly sample the measurement outcomes of the fragile measurement. Take, for example, the fragile observable O1 in Eq. (2). We are not interested directly in the measurement statistics of O1, and only use it to decide whether the conditional S gate is applied or not. However, the Tinjection gadget is deterministic after the conditional S gate is applied: it will always apply a T gate to the input state. Therefore, it doesn’t matter whether we choose the outcome to be +1 or −1, and we can therefore choose it to be +1 without randomly sampling the result. Note that such a trick only works for the first few T-injections in a circuit whose corresponding observables are fragile. What we have described above is only one way of explaining why fragile observables do not need to be decoded. Here we briefly outline an alternative, entirely equivalent way of understanding this procedure. It turns out that for a fragile observable O that is modeled using a coin toss above, any S gates that are conditioned on O can actually be replaced by a Pauli gate conditioned on O. A simple example of this is the S gate conditioned on O1 in Eq. (2): because the T gate is being applied to the |+⟩ state, the conditional S gate can be replaced by a conditional X gate. One can generalize this argument to general circuits and show that this replacement can be done for precisely the same observables that we modeled with a coin toss above. One can then track this conditional X gate in software through the rest of the algorithm, possibly updating future observables to include M1 when they would be flipped by the conditional gate (for example, O2 in Eq. (2)). This last process turns out to be exactly equivalent to the procedure described above of multiplying fragile observables together to make new

C. Issues with hierarchical matching decoding In contrast to the lom decoder introduced above, recent work [17, 19, 20] has used a different strategy to decode transversal Clifford gates in the surface code. We refer to this decoder as the hierarchical matching decoder (it has also been called a sequential or ordered matching decoder). In this section, we explain why such an approach is not fault-tolerant in general, hence justifying our design of the lom decoder. It is worth noting that we do not rule out the possibility that these issues with a hierarchical matching decoder could be overcome; the goal here is simply to point out what issues need to be

We describe the hierarchical matching decoder in the simplified setting of non-conditional Clifford circuit under the basic error model, as this is sufficient to break its fault-tolerance. The hierarchical matching decoder works by splitting the decoding graph G into a number of track subgraphs Tl = (Vl, El) for l = 1, 2, . . . , L, each of which is a graph and is hence matchable. The idea is to decode each track Tl sequentially, starting at l = 1, and committing to a subset of hyperedges in G at each step. More precisely, we define each track by specifying a vertex subset Vl ⊆ V. This vertex subset must satisfy

With Crit. 1, the tracks are defined as Definition 2 (Hierarchical Tracks). For a set of vertex subsets {Vl}l=1,...,L satisfying Crit. 1, the track subgraph Tl is given by Tl = (Vl, El) where the track edges are

We also define the hyperedge subset Hl as the set of hyperedges that correspond to the edges in El. With a set of tracks defined by Def. 2, the hierarchical decoder works by building a correction to the full hypergraph G “hierarchically”; that is, by decoding each track Tl sequentially, starting at l = 1, and committing a subset of hyperedges in G at each step. A simple example is shown in Fig. 8. By the end of the algorithm we will have built a correction ⃗h ⊆ H of the full hypergraph. Note that Crit. 1(c) guarantees that the first track T1 is always matchable. Therefore, we perform matching on

T1, returning a track correction ⃗e1 ⊆ E1. We then commit this correction to the full hypergraph G; that is, for every hyperedge h1 ∈ H1 we commit to its inclusion in the correction ⃗h ⊆ H depending on whether the corresponding edge is in the track correction ⃗e1. Then, we update the remaining defects in the graph, flipping them if they are the endpoint of a hyperedge in the correction ⃗h. By definition, this means that there will be no more defects in the first track, but the update could introduce or remove defects in the later tracks (we call these “artificial” defects). We then continue to the second track T2. Now, note that all hyperedges h with |h ∩ V2| = 1 must satisfy |h ∩ V1| = 2 and therefore must already be committed to. We can then decode the real and artificial defects in T2 using matching on the subgraph with vertices V2 and edges E2. Repeating this process for all l provides a correction to the hypergraph G, from which the logical action can be inferred. At this point it is useful to compare the hierarchical matching decoder to the lom decoder defined in Section III. Indeed, the two decoders are closely related: the region of the hypergraph G decoded in each iteration of the single-lom decoder always forms a valid choice for the first track T1 of a hierarchical matching decoder because the matchable subgraph GO for a logical operator O is a valid first track choice. The difference is that the hierarchical matching decoder then attempts to use this correction from T1 as a starting point for a correction to the full hypergraph G, while the lom decoder does not use the result of T1 at all when decoding other regions of the hypergraph. In fact, the reverse is also (almost) true: any valid choice of first track T1 corresponds to the matchable subgraph GO corresponding to the backpropagation of some operator O, although this operator may not be an actual observable (for example, the operator to be backpropagated could have an X operator immediately preceding Z-measurement). This point can be seen by noting that after fixing a choice of which time-like edges immediately following a logical gate L are included in T1, there is only one valid choice of time-like edges immediately preceding L that can be included in T1. By inspection of Fig. 2, this unique valid choice corresponds to the backpropagation of the corresponding logical Pauli
